A_target.statement:
Let $\map P F$ be a [[Definition:Propositional Function|property]] of finite forests, that is, lists of trees.
Suppose $\map P {\mathsf {nil} }$ holds, and $\map P F \land \map Q t \implies \map P {t :: F}$ for every tree $t$.
Then $\map P F$ holds for every finite forest $F$.

B_source.statement:
Let $\map P t$ be a [[Definition:Propositional Function|property]] of finite binary trees.
Suppose $\map P {\mathsf {leaf} }$ holds, and $\map P l \land \map P r \implies \map P {\map {\mathsf {node} } {l, r} }$.
Then $\map P t$ holds for every finite binary tree $t$, by [[Principle of Structural Induction|structural induction]].

substitutions.tree constructors {leaf, node}: forest constructors {empty, cons of tree and forest}
substitutions.recursion on subtrees: recursion on the head tree and tail forest

derived.induction hypothesis on subtrees: induction hypothesis on head tree (via tree induction) and tail forest

validity_conditions: Forests are freely generated by {empty, cons}, and trees and forests are mutually recursive, so simultaneous structural induction is valid.
The head-tree obligation is discharged by tree induction; the tail-forest obligation by the forest induction hypothesis - the same base-plus-constructor-step skeleton.
proof_plan: The constructors for forests are $\mathsf {nil}$ and $t :: F$.
Map the tree skeleton of a base case and a constructor step onto forests: the base case is $\map P {\mathsf {nil} }$.
In the step for $t :: F$, use the tree induction hypothesis $\map Q t$ for the head and the forest hypothesis $\map P F$ for the tail.

Hence forest induction follows the same [[Principle of Structural Induction|structural induction]] plan.
{{qed}}
